supplier_excerpts.quote:
Input: a finite expression DAG, a closed interval/rectangle domain box $X$, a
dyadic requested width $\varepsilon>0$, finite-format parameters, series
truncation index $N\ge1$, and integer total box-split budget $B\ge0$. Set a shared counter
$R:=B$ and a queue containing $X$. Process boxes in a fixed order. For each
box $Q$, evaluate the DAG by
[[alg-certified-elementary-range-evaluation]] with the same format and $N$.

- If evaluation returns a non-finite status, return that status and the exact
  unresolved box $Q$; it is not a tolerance certificate.
- If it returns a finite enclosure $I$ with width at most $\varepsilon$, save
  $I$ as a completed leaf enclosure.
- If it returns a finite enclosure wider than $\varepsilon$ and $R=0$, return
  `inconclusive` with the completed-leaf hull, $Q$, and the unmet width test.
- If it returns a finite enclosure wider than $\varepsilon$ and $R>0$, select
  a widest nondegenerate input coordinate (breaking ties by the first
  coordinate in the input order), split it at its dyadic midpoint
  into two closed halves, decrement the shared counter $R$ by one, and append
  both halves to the queue. If no coordinate can be split, return
  `inconclusive` with the unmet width test.

When the queue is empty, take the hull $J$ of all completed leaf enclosures.
Return `certified(J,X)` only if $\operatorname{width}(J)\le\varepsilon$;
otherwise return `inconclusive(J,X)` and state that the global width test
failed. Each split covers its parent because the two closed halves overlap at
the midpoint and their union is the parent coordinate interval. The shared
counter makes $B$ a total split limit across the full computation.

For every finite input DAG and finite total split budget $B$, the algorithm
[[alg-budgeted-validated-range-evaluation]] terminates. If it returns
`certified(I,X)`, then $I$ contains the exact function range on all of $X$ and
has width at most the requested $\varepsilon$. If it returns `inconclusive`,
domain error, split-domain, or overflow, it makes no unconditional
tolerance-success claim.

supplier_excerpts.quote: Input an exact rational $q$, a target $0<\tau\le1/4$, a dyadic exponent range, an initial precision $p_0\ge2$, a finite precision cap $p_{\max}\ge p_0$, and a finite elementary-series cap. The target value is $w=e^{\pi iq}=\cos(\pi q)+i\sin(\pi q)$ for the canonical Fourier $\pi$, identified with the interval evaluator's constant by [[thm-na-interval-pi-matches-canonical-fourier-pi]]. For precision $p=p_0,p_0+1,\ldots,p_{\max}$, build the finite expression DAG for $\cos(\pi q)$ and $\sin(\pi q)$, with rational constants enclosed by directed dyadic rounding, and call [[alg-certified-elementary-range-evaluation]] with that precision and series cap; its fixed finite-cell rules govern range reduction. If either result is non-finite, continue at the next precision unless the precision cap is reached, in which case return `inconclusive` with the supplier status. If the results are finite intervals $C=[c_-,c_+]$ and $S=[s_-,s_+]$, set $\widehat w=c_-+is_-$ and compute an upward-rounded dyadic $\epsilon\ge(c_+-c_-)+(s_+-s_-)$. If $\epsilon\le\tau$, return `certified(\widehat w,\epsilon)`; otherwise continue or return `inconclusive` at the cap. A non-finite endpoint or overflow returns its explicit failure status. The routine makes no finite-error claim on a failure branch.
Whenever [[alg-na-certified-unit-circle-phase]] returns `certified(\widehat w,\epsilon)` on rational input $q$, its output satisfies $|\widehat w-e^{\pi iq}|\le\epsilon\le\tau$.

supplier_excerpts.quote:
Let the representable set, normal range, and unit roundoff be as in [[def-standard-relative-floating-point-model-and-unit-roundoff]]. Here fl is round-to-nearest, ties-to-even, on each real exact result that is zero or normal; every other nonzero exact result (subnormal or overflow), NaN, infinity, invalid operation, or division by zero returns range-failure. A real add, subtract, multiply, or divide is one rounded operation. For positive in-range x, fl(sqrt(x)) is correctly rounded to nearest, ties-to-even, and fails unless its result is positive and normal. A real fused multiply-add returns the correctly rounded value of the single exact expression ab+c; it is not two operations.

Complex addition and subtraction round real and imaginary components separately. A complex product (a+ib)(c+id) uses four rounded real products ac, bd, ad, bc, then rounded subtraction and addition, for six real operations. Conjugation and sign changes are exact. Scaling and division by a positive real scalar round each complex component separately; no other complex division primitive is used here.

A procedure succeeds only when each exact intermediate is zero or normal and every rounded output is finite; otherwise it returns the first range-failure with its operation or pivot index. For ku<1 write gamma_k=ku/(1-ku). This is a no-underflow success model, not the gradual-underflow model.

originalContainer.required_interface: The supplier defines arctan x as the integral from 0 to x of 1/(1+t^2) and states pi=4 arctan(1). The new local proof identifies that value with the canonical pi used by the published finite Fourier transform.

supplier_excerpts.quote:
Every integral below is the oriented Riemann integral constructed from upper
and lower Darboux sums in
[[lem-continuous-functions-riemann-integrable]]. It exists for each displayed
continuous integrand on the finite interval between its endpoints, is additive
in intervals, reverses sign when the endpoints are reversed, is monotone in
the integrand, and satisfies
$|\int_a^b g(t)\,dt|\le|b-a|\max_{t\text{ between }a\text{ and }b}|g(t)|$.
These properties also
give constant comparison bounds and the average-value difference quotient
used to differentiate the integral-defined functions.

The exponential is $\exp(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}x^k/k!$ for $x\in\mathbb R$.
The sine and cosine are the everywhere-convergent power series
$\sin x=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(-1)^k x^{2k+1}/(2k+1)!$ and
$\cos x=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(-1)^k x^{2k}/(2k)!$. Define
$\arctan x=\int_0^x dt/(1+t^2)$ and set $\pi=4\arctan1$. The natural
logarithm $\ln$ is defined on $(0,\infty)$ by $\ln x=\int_1^x dt/t$.

The square root is the unique nonnegative real $y$ with $y^2=x$ for $x\ge0$;
existence and uniqueness follow from
[[lem-nonnegative-square-root-exists-and-unique]]. The tangent is
$\tan x=\sin x/\cos x$ on the set where $\cos x\ne0$.

For complex $z=x+iy$, the modulus $|z|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ is defined in
[[def-intervals-rectangles-and-complex-balls]]. The complex exponential is
$\exp(x+iy)=\exp(x)(\cos y+i\sin y)$. The principal complex logarithm is
$\operatorname{Log}(z)=\ln|z|+i\operatorname{Arg}(z)$ on
$\mathbb C\setminus(-\infty,0]$. For $z=x+iy$ in this domain, define
$$
\operatorname{Arg}(x+iy)=
\begin{cases}
\arctan(y/x),&x>0,\\
\pi/2,&x=0,\ y>0,\\
-\pi/2,&x=0,\ y<0,\\
\pi-\arctan(y/(-x)),&x<0,\ y>0,\\
-\pi+\arctan((-y)/(-x)),&x<0,\ y<0.
\end{cases}
$$
The excluded negative real axis is the remaining case $x<0,y=0$; zero is
also excluded.

These are point functions. An interval extension must separately enclose their
exact ranges, test the stated domains, and return a non-finite status when its
finite budget cannot certify a reduction or endpoint.

supplier_excerpts.quote:
An exact dyadic rational is a number $m2^q$ with integers $m,q$.
Fix integers $p\ge2$ and $e_{\min}\le e_{\max}$. Put
$\eta=2^{e_{\min}-p+1}$ and
$N_{\max}=(2^p-1)2^{e_{\max}-p+1}$. The finite representable set $\mathbb F$
consists of zero, both signs of every normal number $k2^{e-p+1}$ with
$e_{\min}\le e\le e_{\max}$ and $2^{p-1}\le k<2^p$, and both signs of every
subnormal number $k\eta$ with $1\le k<2^{p-1}$. The smallest positive
subnormal is $\eta$, the smallest positive normal is $2^{e_{\min}}$, and the
largest finite magnitude is $N_{\max}$. The extended endpoint set also contains
$-\infty$ and $+\infty$ as enclosure sentinels; they are not finite machine
numbers.

For a real $x$ with $|x|\le N_{\max}$, define $\operatorname{rd}(x)$ as the
greatest member of $\mathbb F$ not exceeding $x$, and $\operatorname{ru}(x)$ as
the least member of $\mathbb F$ not less than $x$. Define
$\rho(x)=\operatorname{ru}(x)-\operatorname{rd}(x)$. For nonzero $x$ in the
subnormal range, define the absolute-error bound $\epsilon_{\rm abs}(x)=\eta$;
for $2^e\le |x|<2^{e+1}$ in the normal range, define
$\epsilon_{\rm abs}(x)=2^{e-p+2}$. At finite overflow, a directed result is
the corresponding infinite sentinel and its error bound is $+\infty$; the
status is `overflow`. The rounding procedure reports `finite`, `subnormal`, or
`overflow`, so no relative-error assumption is implicit.

An exact rational intermediate may be converted by comparing integer
numerators and denominators after clearing powers of two. A directed interval
endpoint is the resulting greatest lower or least upper member of $\mathbb F$.

A **real interval** is a closed set $[a,b]\subset\mathbb R$ with finite dyadic
endpoints $a\le b$. Its width is $b-a$, midpoint is $(a+b)/2$, and its
midpoint-radius form is $m+[-r,r]$ with $m=(a+b)/2$ and $r=(b-a)/2$. The empty
set is the status `empty`; the whole real line is `entire`. `overflow`,
`domain-error`, `split-domain`, and `inconclusive` are computation statuses,
not finite intervals.

A **complex rectangle** is $X+iY=\{x+iy:x\in X,\ y\in Y\}$ for real intervals
$X,Y$. Complex addition and multiplication use
$(x+iy)+(u+iv)=(x+u)+i(y+v)$ and
$(x+iy)(u+iv)=(xu-yv)+i(xv+yu)$. For $z=x+iy$, its complex modulus is
$|z|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$, and for $z\ne0$ its reciprocal is
$1/z=(x-iy)/(x^2+y^2)$. A
**complex ball** $B(c,r)$ is
$\{z\in\mathbb C:|z-c|\le r\}$ with dyadic complex center $c$ and dyadic
$r\ge0$. For any two represented sets $S,T$, the inclusion order is
$S\sqsubseteq T$ iff $S\subseteq T$.

The width of a complex rectangle with coordinate widths $w_X,w_Y$ is its
Euclidean diameter $\sqrt{w_X^2+w_Y^2}$; the width of a ball $B(c,r)$ is its
diameter $2r$. Width comparisons against a dyadic tolerance can be decided by
exact rational comparisons after squaring the nonnegative quantities.

The **range** of a real or complex function $f$ on a set $S$ is
$f(S)=\{f(x):x\in S\cap\operatorname{dom}(f)\}$. A finite expression DAG is a
finite directed acyclic graph with input nodes, constant nodes, and operation
nodes; constants are exact dyadics or are supplied with certified enclosing
intervals. Sharing a node means the exact same intermediate value is reused.

For real intervals $X=[a,b]$ and $Y=[c,d]$, compute the displayed exact
endpoint formulas and round the lower endpoint down and the upper endpoint up
in the format of
[[def-dyadic-floating-point-format-and-directed-rounding]]. If either exact
endpoint overflows, return `overflow` with the outward extended endpoints;
never substitute a finite endpoint for an overflow sentinel. Addition is
$[a+c,b+d]$, subtraction is $[a-d,b-c]$, and multiplication is
$[\min(ac,ad,bc,bd),\max(ac,ad,bc,bd)]$. Division is defined only when
$0\notin Y$ and is $X[1/d,1/c]$, with reciprocal endpoints computed as exact
rationals before outward rounding. Squaring is
$[0,\max(a^2,b^2)]$ when $0\in X$ and
$[\min(a^2,b^2),\max(a^2,b^2)]$ otherwise. Square root is defined only for
$X\subseteq[0,\infty)$ and is enclosed by applying
[[alg-dyadic-square-root-bisection]] to the exact dyadic endpoints with
request $n=p$, where $p$ is the selected format precision, and rounding
outward for storage.

If $0\in Y$ for division, return `split-domain` with the two subdomains
$Y\cap(-\infty,0)$ and $Y\cap(0,\infty)$, or `entire` when the caller does not
request subdivision. No finite quotient interval is returned in this case.
An invalid square-root domain returns `domain-error` or an explicitly
restricted nonnegative subdomain.

Complex-rectangle addition, subtraction and multiplication use
$(x+iy)(u+iv)=(xu-yv)+i(xv+yu)$, applying the real interval operations to
each component. For a rectangle $X+iY$ excluding $0$, define its reciprocal by
$(X-iY)/(X^2+Y^2)$; the denominator interval is strictly positive because at
least one coordinate interval excludes zero. Division multiplies by this
reciprocal.

For a ball $B(c,r)$, let $X_B=[\Re c-r,\Re c+r]$ and
$Y_B=[\Im c-r,\Im c+r]$ be its coordinate projection intervals. For a real
interval $J$, let $M(J)=\max(|\inf J|,|\sup J|)$ and let $d(J)=0$ if
$0\in J$, otherwise $d(J)=\min(|\inf J|,|\sup J|)$. Put
$M_B=M(X_B)+M(Y_B)$ and $m_B=\max(d(X_B),d(Y_B))$. Then
$|z|\le M_B$ for every $z\in B(c,r)$ and $|z|\ge m_B$ for every such $z$.
Define ball addition and subtraction as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}+M_{B_2}))$, multiplication as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}M_{B_2}))$, and division as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}/m_{B_2}))$ only when $m_{B_2}>0$. These
origin-centered output balls are conservative but inclusion-isotone. If
$m_{B_2}=0$, return `split-domain`, `entire`, or `inconclusive`; if a radius
overlows, return `overflow`.

Every integral below is the oriented Riemann integral constructed from upper
and lower Darboux sums in
[[lem-continuous-functions-riemann-integrable]]. It exists for each displayed
continuous integrand on the finite interval between its endpoints, is additive
in intervals, reverses sign when the endpoints are reversed, is monotone in
the integrand, and satisfies
$|\int_a^b g(t)\,dt|\le|b-a|\max_{t\text{ between }a\text{ and }b}|g(t)|$.
These properties also
give constant comparison bounds and the average-value difference quotient
used to differentiate the integral-defined functions.

The exponential is $\exp(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}x^k/k!$ for $x\in\mathbb R$.
The sine and cosine are the everywhere-convergent power series
$\sin x=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(-1)^k x^{2k+1}/(2k+1)!$ and
$\cos x=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(-1)^k x^{2k}/(2k)!$. Define
$\arctan x=\int_0^x dt/(1+t^2)$ and set $\pi=4\arctan1$. The natural
logarithm $\ln$ is defined on $(0,\infty)$ by $\ln x=\int_1^x dt/t$.

The square root is the unique nonnegative real $y$ with $y^2=x$ for $x\ge0$;
existence and uniqueness follow from
[[lem-nonnegative-square-root-exists-and-unique]]. The tangent is
$\tan x=\sin x/\cos x$ on the set where $\cos x\ne0$.

For complex $z=x+iy$, the modulus $|z|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ is defined in
[[def-intervals-rectangles-and-complex-balls]]. The complex exponential is
$\exp(x+iy)=\exp(x)(\cos y+i\sin y)$. The principal complex logarithm is
$\operatorname{Log}(z)=\ln|z|+i\operatorname{Arg}(z)$ on
$\mathbb C\setminus(-\infty,0]$. For $z=x+iy$ in this domain, define
$$
\operatorname{Arg}(x+iy)=
\begin{cases}
\arctan(y/x),&x>0,\\
\pi/2,&x=0,\ y>0,\\
-\pi/2,&x=0,\ y<0,\\
\pi-\arctan(y/(-x)),&x<0,\ y>0,\\
-\pi+\arctan((-y)/(-x)),&x<0,\ y<0.
\end{cases}
$$
The excluded negative real axis is the remaining case $x<0,y=0$; zero is
also excluded.

These are point functions. An interval extension must separately enclose their
exact ranges, test the stated domains, and return a non-finite status when its
finite budget cannot certify a reduction or endpoint.

Input: a finite expression DAG with real interval or complex rectangle input,
a finite dyadic format and an integer truncation index $N\ge1$. All constants,
including the Machin enclosure of $\pi$, use the same fixed $N$ and format
throughout a call. Output: a finite interval/rectangle enclosure, or one of
`empty`, `domain-error`, `split-domain`, `overflow`, or `inconclusive` with the
unresolved domain piece. No value from a system `libm` routine is treated as a
certified endpoint.

1. Evaluate arithmetic nodes by
[[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]]. On an invalid divisor
return its declared status. For $\sqrt{X}$ require $X\subseteq[0,\infty)$; for
$\ln X$ require $X\subseteq(0,\infty)$. If an input is not wholly in the
stated domain, return `domain-error` rather than silently discarding points.

2. Set $s=\max(0,e_{\max}+2)$, using the exponent in
[[def-dyadic-floating-point-format-and-directed-rounding]]. Since
$N_{\max}<2^{e_{\max}+1}$, exact dyadic comparison gives
$N_{\max}/2^s<1/2$. For an
interval $X$, evaluate the truncated exponential polynomial on $U=X/2^s$ by
interval arithmetic, add the symmetric tail using $\max_{u\in U}|u|$, then
square the resulting interval $s$ times. If its lower endpoint is not
positive or an endpoint overflows, return `inconclusive` or `overflow`. For
$\ln$, split $X\subset(0,\infty)$ into its intersections with the fixed
dyadic bins $[2^j,2^{j+1}]$. On each nonempty piece set
$Y=2^{-j}X_j\subseteq[1,2]$, $V=(Y-1)/(Y+1)$, evaluate the positive logarithm
series on $V$ with its tail determined by $\max|V|$, and combine
$j\ln2+\ln Y$ by outward arithmetic. Take the hull over all intersected
bins.

3. Partition $\arctan$ input at the fixed real breakpoints
$-3,-1/2,1/2,3$. On pieces within $[-1/2,1/2]$, use its alternating power
series interval evaluation. For $t\in[1/2,1]$, use
$\arctan t=\pi/4-\arctan((1-t)/(1+t))$; for $t\in[1,3]$, use
$\arctan t=\pi/4+\arctan((t-1)/(t+1))$; for $t>3$, use
$\arctan t=\pi/2-\arctan(1/t)$. Use odd symmetry on negative pieces.
Enclose $\pi$ by Machin's identity and the alternating series at $1/5$ and
$1/239$, forming their rational partial sums and tail endpoints exactly
before the final outward conversion. If any branch test is unresolved, return
`inconclusive`.

4. For sine and cosine, first compute one outward Machin interval $P_N$ for
$\pi$ using the same $N$ and format, with the rational series endpoints
combined exactly before final outward conversion. If $P_N$ is non-finite or
its lower endpoint is not positive, return `inconclusive`. For finite input
$X=[a,b]$, put $M_X=\max(|a|,|b|)$, $p_-:=\inf(P_N)>0$, and
$K=\lceil2M_X/p_-\rceil+1$, with the ceiling computed by exact rational
comparisons. For $k>K$, the outward lower endpoint of cell $k$ is
$(2k-1)p_-/4>M_X$; for $k<-K$, its outward upper endpoint is
$-(2|k|-1)p_-/4<-M_X$. Thus every cell enclosure that can intersect $X$ is
in the finite candidate list $-K,\ldots,K$. Use the fixed canonical cells
$[k\pi/2-\pi/4,k\pi/2+\pi/4]$, $k\in\mathbb Z$. Enclose each cell using
exact rational expressions from $P_N$ and let $X_k$ be the interval hull of
its intersection with $X$; do not round candidate-cell or residual endpoints.
Include every cell whose $P_N$ enclosure cannot be ruled out as intersecting
$X$. Certify the residual enclosure $R=X_k-kP_N/2$ satisfies
$R\subseteq[-1,1]$, evaluate the corresponding power
polynomial and add the explicit geometric tail by exact rational interval
arithmetic, then round the final endpoints outward. The tail comes from
[[lem-trigonometric-identities-machin-and-range-reduction]], and map by the
quarter-period identities. Intersect every finite sine/cosine enclosure
with $[-1,1]$, including after the sign and coordinate swaps; the exact
values satisfy these bounds. If the input width is at least $2\sup(P_N)$,
return $[-1,1]$. If a cell cannot be certified in the reduced interval or the
finite candidate list cannot be resolved, return `inconclusive`. For tangent,
divide the sine enclosure by the cosine enclosure only on canonical pieces
where the latter excludes zero; otherwise return `split-domain` or
`inconclusive`.

5. For complex exponential, evaluate real $\exp(X)$, $\cos(Y)$ and
$\sin(Y)$ and combine them by rectangle operations. For principal
$\operatorname{Log}$, require a rectangle excluding zero and every point of
the negative real branch cut; otherwise return `domain-error`. Subdivide into
sign-stable quadrants and axis pieces; on the quadrants use
$$
\operatorname{Arg}(x+iy)=
\begin{cases}
\arctan(y/x),&x>0,\ y>0,\\
-\arctan((-y)/x),&x>0,\ y<0,\\
\pi-\arctan(y/(-x)),&x<0,\ y>0,\\
-\pi+\arctan((-y)/(-x)),&x<0,\ y<0.
\end{cases}
$$
For $x=0,y>0$ set $\operatorname{Arg}(iy)=\pi/2$, for $x=0,y<0$ set it to
$-\pi/2$, and on the positive real axis set it to zero. Enclose
$\ln\sqrt{X^2+Y^2}$ by the real operations and elementary evaluators. If the
branch or sign cannot be certified, return `inconclusive`.

6. Each displayed series uses indices $0,\ldots,N$, hence at most $N+1$
terms; $N$ is the truncation index. Branch breakpoints, dyadic scales and
$P_N$ are fixed by the call parameters, independent of the input box; no
adaptive subdivision or precision refinement is hidden inside this evaluator.

Every finite enclosure returned by
[[alg-certified-elementary-range-evaluation]] for a real interval in the
domain of $\exp$, $\ln$, $\sqrt{\phantom{x}}$, $\arctan$, $\sin$, $\cos$, or
$\tan$ contains the exact range of that function on the represented domain.
If two input intervals are nested and both calls return finite enclosures,
the canonical branch-cell and fixed-term construction in the algorithm makes
the smaller interval's computed enclosure a subset of the larger one's.
An unresolved fixed branch, pole, invalid domain or overflow returns its
stated non-finite status and carries no finite success claim.

For real intervals, complex rectangles or complex balls on which an operation
is defined, enlarging either input enclosure cannot shrink the computed
enclosure: for binary $\circ\in\{+,-,\times,\div\}$, if $X\subseteq X'$ and
$Y\subseteq Y'$, then the computed set enclosure of $X\circ Y$ is contained
in that of $X'\circ Y'$ whenever both are finite results and their domain
restrictions are preserved. The square-root enclosure is inclusion-isotone on
nonnegative intervals. Each finite ball operation in
[[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]] contains the exact ball
image. A `split-domain`, `entire`, `domain-error`, `overflow`, or
`inconclusive` status makes no finite claim. For a finite expression DAG
whose operation nodes all return finite enclosures, every exact node value
from every admissible input assignment belongs to its computed node
enclosure; in particular, the root enclosure contains the exact range. If any
node returns a non-finite status, no finite DAG enclosure is asserted.

endpoints $a\le b$. Its width is $b-a$, midpoint is $(a+b)/2$, and its
midpoint-radius form is $m+[-r,r]$ with $m=(a+b)/2$ and $r=(b-a)/2$. The empty
set is the status `empty`; the whole real line is `entire`. `overflow`,
`domain-error`, `split-domain`, and `inconclusive` are computation statuses,
not finite intervals.

A **complex rectangle** is $X+iY=\{x+iy:x\in X,\ y\in Y\}$ for real intervals
$X,Y$. Complex addition and multiplication use
$(x+iy)+(u+iv)=(x+u)+i(y+v)$ and
$(x+iy)(u+iv)=(xu-yv)+i(xv+yu)$. For $z=x+iy$, its complex modulus is
$|z|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$, and for $z\ne0$ its reciprocal is
$1/z=(x-iy)/(x^2+y^2)$. A
**complex ball** $B(c,r)$ is
$\{z\in\mathbb C:|z-c|\le r\}$ with dyadic complex center $c$ and dyadic
$r\ge0$. For any two represented sets $S,T$, the inclusion order is
$S\sqsubseteq T$ iff $S\subseteq T$.

The width of a complex rectangle with coordinate widths $w_X,w_Y$ is its
Euclidean diameter $\sqrt{w_X^2+w_Y^2}$; the width of a ball $B(c,r)$ is its
diameter $2r$. Width comparisons against a dyadic tolerance can be decided by
exact rational comparisons after squaring the nonnegative quantities.

$f(S)=\{f(x):x\in S\cap\operatorname{dom}(f)\}$. A finite expression DAG is a

nodes; constants are exact dyadics or are supplied with certified enclosing

supplier_excerpts.quote:
Let the representable set, normal range, and unit roundoff be as in [[def-standard-relative-floating-point-model-and-unit-roundoff]]. Here fl is round-to-nearest, ties-to-even, on each real exact result that is zero or normal; every other nonzero exact result (subnormal or overflow), NaN, infinity, invalid operation, or division by zero returns range-failure. A real add, subtract, multiply, or divide is one rounded operation. For positive in-range x, fl(sqrt(x)) is correctly rounded to nearest, ties-to-even, and fails unless its result is positive and normal. A real fused multiply-add returns the correctly rounded value of the single exact expression ab+c; it is not two operations.

Complex addition and subtraction round real and imaginary components separately. A complex product (a+ib)(c+id) uses four rounded real products ac, bd, ad, bc, then rounded subtraction and addition, for six real operations. Conjugation and sign changes are exact. Scaling and division by a positive real scalar round each complex component separately; no other complex division primitive is used here.

A procedure succeeds only when each exact intermediate is zero or normal and every rounded output is finite; otherwise it returns the first range-failure with its operation or pivot index. For ku<1 write gamma_k=ku/(1-ku). This is a no-underflow success model, not the gradual-underflow model.

supplier_excerpts.quote:
An exact dyadic rational is a number $m2^q$ with integers $m,q$.
Fix integers $p\ge2$ and $e_{\min}\le e_{\max}$. Put
$\eta=2^{e_{\min}-p+1}$ and
$N_{\max}=(2^p-1)2^{e_{\max}-p+1}$. The finite representable set $\mathbb F$
consists of zero, both signs of every normal number $k2^{e-p+1}$ with
$e_{\min}\le e\le e_{\max}$ and $2^{p-1}\le k<2^p$, and both signs of every
subnormal number $k\eta$ with $1\le k<2^{p-1}$. The smallest positive
subnormal is $\eta$, the smallest positive normal is $2^{e_{\min}}$, and the
largest finite magnitude is $N_{\max}$. The extended endpoint set also contains
$-\infty$ and $+\infty$ as enclosure sentinels; they are not finite machine
numbers.

For a real $x$ with $|x|\le N_{\max}$, define $\operatorname{rd}(x)$ as the
greatest member of $\mathbb F$ not exceeding $x$, and $\operatorname{ru}(x)$ as
the least member of $\mathbb F$ not less than $x$. Define
$\rho(x)=\operatorname{ru}(x)-\operatorname{rd}(x)$. For nonzero $x$ in the
subnormal range, define the absolute-error bound $\epsilon_{\rm abs}(x)=\eta$;
for $2^e\le |x|<2^{e+1}$ in the normal range, define
$\epsilon_{\rm abs}(x)=2^{e-p+2}$. At finite overflow, a directed result is
the corresponding infinite sentinel and its error bound is $+\infty$; the
status is `overflow`. The rounding procedure reports `finite`, `subnormal`, or
`overflow`, so no relative-error assumption is implicit.

An exact rational intermediate may be converted by comparing integer
numerators and denominators after clearing powers of two. A directed interval
endpoint is the resulting greatest lower or least upper member of $\mathbb F$.

A **real interval** is a closed set $[a,b]\subset\mathbb R$ with finite dyadic
endpoints $a\le b$. Its width is $b-a$, midpoint is $(a+b)/2$, and its
midpoint-radius form is $m+[-r,r]$ with $m=(a+b)/2$ and $r=(b-a)/2$. The empty
set is the status `empty`; the whole real line is `entire`. `overflow`,
`domain-error`, `split-domain`, and `inconclusive` are computation statuses,
not finite intervals.

A **complex rectangle** is $X+iY=\{x+iy:x\in X,\ y\in Y\}$ for real intervals
$X,Y$. Complex addition and multiplication use
$(x+iy)+(u+iv)=(x+u)+i(y+v)$ and
$(x+iy)(u+iv)=(xu-yv)+i(xv+yu)$. For $z=x+iy$, its complex modulus is
$|z|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$, and for $z\ne0$ its reciprocal is
$1/z=(x-iy)/(x^2+y^2)$. A
**complex ball** $B(c,r)$ is
$\{z\in\mathbb C:|z-c|\le r\}$ with dyadic complex center $c$ and dyadic
$r\ge0$. For any two represented sets $S,T$, the inclusion order is
$S\sqsubseteq T$ iff $S\subseteq T$.

The width of a complex rectangle with coordinate widths $w_X,w_Y$ is its
Euclidean diameter $\sqrt{w_X^2+w_Y^2}$; the width of a ball $B(c,r)$ is its
diameter $2r$. Width comparisons against a dyadic tolerance can be decided by
exact rational comparisons after squaring the nonnegative quantities.

The **range** of a real or complex function $f$ on a set $S$ is
$f(S)=\{f(x):x\in S\cap\operatorname{dom}(f)\}$. A finite expression DAG is a
finite directed acyclic graph with input nodes, constant nodes, and operation
nodes; constants are exact dyadics or are supplied with certified enclosing
intervals. Sharing a node means the exact same intermediate value is reused.

For real intervals $X=[a,b]$ and $Y=[c,d]$, compute the displayed exact
endpoint formulas and round the lower endpoint down and the upper endpoint up
in the format of
[[def-dyadic-floating-point-format-and-directed-rounding]]. If either exact
endpoint overflows, return `overflow` with the outward extended endpoints;
never substitute a finite endpoint for an overflow sentinel. Addition is
$[a+c,b+d]$, subtraction is $[a-d,b-c]$, and multiplication is
$[\min(ac,ad,bc,bd),\max(ac,ad,bc,bd)]$. Division is defined only when
$0\notin Y$ and is $X[1/d,1/c]$, with reciprocal endpoints computed as exact
rationals before outward rounding. Squaring is
$[0,\max(a^2,b^2)]$ when $0\in X$ and
$[\min(a^2,b^2),\max(a^2,b^2)]$ otherwise. Square root is defined only for
$X\subseteq[0,\infty)$ and is enclosed by applying
[[alg-dyadic-square-root-bisection]] to the exact dyadic endpoints with
request $n=p$, where $p$ is the selected format precision, and rounding
outward for storage.

If $0\in Y$ for division, return `split-domain` with the two subdomains
$Y\cap(-\infty,0)$ and $Y\cap(0,\infty)$, or `entire` when the caller does not
request subdivision. No finite quotient interval is returned in this case.
An invalid square-root domain returns `domain-error` or an explicitly
restricted nonnegative subdomain.

Complex-rectangle addition, subtraction and multiplication use
$(x+iy)(u+iv)=(xu-yv)+i(xv+yu)$, applying the real interval operations to
each component. For a rectangle $X+iY$ excluding $0$, define its reciprocal by
$(X-iY)/(X^2+Y^2)$; the denominator interval is strictly positive because at
least one coordinate interval excludes zero. Division multiplies by this
reciprocal.

For a ball $B(c,r)$, let $X_B=[\Re c-r,\Re c+r]$ and
$Y_B=[\Im c-r,\Im c+r]$ be its coordinate projection intervals. For a real
interval $J$, let $M(J)=\max(|\inf J|,|\sup J|)$ and let $d(J)=0$ if
$0\in J$, otherwise $d(J)=\min(|\inf J|,|\sup J|)$. Put
$M_B=M(X_B)+M(Y_B)$ and $m_B=\max(d(X_B),d(Y_B))$. Then
$|z|\le M_B$ for every $z\in B(c,r)$ and $|z|\ge m_B$ for every such $z$.
Define ball addition and subtraction as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}+M_{B_2}))$, multiplication as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}M_{B_2}))$, and division as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}/m_{B_2}))$ only when $m_{B_2}>0$. These
origin-centered output balls are conservative but inclusion-isotone. If
$m_{B_2}=0$, return `split-domain`, `entire`, or `inconclusive`; if a radius
overlows, return `overflow`.

Every integral below is the oriented Riemann integral constructed from upper
and lower Darboux sums in
[[lem-continuous-functions-riemann-integrable]]. It exists for each displayed
continuous integrand on the finite interval between its endpoints, is additive
in intervals, reverses sign when the endpoints are reversed, is monotone in
the integrand, and satisfies
$|\int_a^b g(t)\,dt|\le|b-a|\max_{t\text{ between }a\text{ and }b}|g(t)|$.
These properties also
give constant comparison bounds and the average-value difference quotient
used to differentiate the integral-defined functions.

The exponential is $\exp(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}x^k/k!$ for $x\in\mathbb R$.
The sine and cosine are the everywhere-convergent power series
$\sin x=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(-1)^k x^{2k+1}/(2k+1)!$ and
$\cos x=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(-1)^k x^{2k}/(2k)!$. Define
$\arctan x=\int_0^x dt/(1+t^2)$ and set $\pi=4\arctan1$. The natural
logarithm $\ln$ is defined on $(0,\infty)$ by $\ln x=\int_1^x dt/t$.

The square root is the unique nonnegative real $y$ with $y^2=x$ for $x\ge0$;
existence and uniqueness follow from
[[lem-nonnegative-square-root-exists-and-unique]]. The tangent is
$\tan x=\sin x/\cos x$ on the set where $\cos x\ne0$.

For complex $z=x+iy$, the modulus $|z|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ is defined in
[[def-intervals-rectangles-and-complex-balls]]. The complex exponential is
$\exp(x+iy)=\exp(x)(\cos y+i\sin y)$. The principal complex logarithm is
$\operatorname{Log}(z)=\ln|z|+i\operatorname{Arg}(z)$ on
$\mathbb C\setminus(-\infty,0]$. For $z=x+iy$ in this domain, define
$$
\operatorname{Arg}(x+iy)=
\begin{cases}
\arctan(y/x),&x>0,\\
\pi/2,&x=0,\ y>0,\\
-\pi/2,&x=0,\ y<0,\\
\pi-\arctan(y/(-x)),&x<0,\ y>0,\\
-\pi+\arctan((-y)/(-x)),&x<0,\ y<0.
\end{cases}
$$
The excluded negative real axis is the remaining case $x<0,y=0$; zero is
also excluded.

These are point functions. An interval extension must separately enclose their
exact ranges, test the stated domains, and return a non-finite status when its
finite budget cannot certify a reduction or endpoint.

Input: a finite expression DAG with real interval or complex rectangle input,
a finite dyadic format and an integer truncation index $N\ge1$. All constants,
including the Machin enclosure of $\pi$, use the same fixed $N$ and format
throughout a call. Output: a finite interval/rectangle enclosure, or one of
`empty`, `domain-error`, `split-domain`, `overflow`, or `inconclusive` with the
unresolved domain piece. No value from a system `libm` routine is treated as a
certified endpoint.

1. Evaluate arithmetic nodes by
[[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]]. On an invalid divisor
return its declared status. For $\sqrt{X}$ require $X\subseteq[0,\infty)$; for
$\ln X$ require $X\subseteq(0,\infty)$. If an input is not wholly in the
stated domain, return `domain-error` rather than silently discarding points.

2. Set $s=\max(0,e_{\max}+2)$, using the exponent in
[[def-dyadic-floating-point-format-and-directed-rounding]]. Since
$N_{\max}<2^{e_{\max}+1}$, exact dyadic comparison gives
$N_{\max}/2^s<1/2$. For an
interval $X$, evaluate the truncated exponential polynomial on $U=X/2^s$ by
interval arithmetic, add the symmetric tail using $\max_{u\in U}|u|$, then
square the resulting interval $s$ times. If its lower endpoint is not
positive or an endpoint overflows, return `inconclusive` or `overflow`. For
$\ln$, split $X\subset(0,\infty)$ into its intersections with the fixed
dyadic bins $[2^j,2^{j+1}]$. On each nonempty piece set
$Y=2^{-j}X_j\subseteq[1,2]$, $V=(Y-1)/(Y+1)$, evaluate the positive logarithm
series on $V$ with its tail determined by $\max|V|$, and combine
$j\ln2+\ln Y$ by outward arithmetic. Take the hull over all intersected
bins.

3. Partition $\arctan$ input at the fixed real breakpoints
$-3,-1/2,1/2,3$. On pieces within $[-1/2,1/2]$, use its alternating power
series interval evaluation. For $t\in[1/2,1]$, use
$\arctan t=\pi/4-\arctan((1-t)/(1+t))$; for $t\in[1,3]$, use
$\arctan t=\pi/4+\arctan((t-1)/(t+1))$; for $t>3$, use
$\arctan t=\pi/2-\arctan(1/t)$. Use odd symmetry on negative pieces.
Enclose $\pi$ by Machin's identity and the alternating series at $1/5$ and
$1/239$, forming their rational partial sums and tail endpoints exactly
before the final outward conversion. If any branch test is unresolved, return
`inconclusive`.

4. For sine and cosine, first compute one outward Machin interval $P_N$ for
$\pi$ using the same $N$ and format, with the rational series endpoints
combined exactly before final outward conversion. If $P_N$ is non-finite or
its lower endpoint is not positive, return `inconclusive`. For finite input
$X=[a,b]$, put $M_X=\max(|a|,|b|)$, $p_-:=\inf(P_N)>0$, and
$K=\lceil2M_X/p_-\rceil+1$, with the ceiling computed by exact rational
comparisons. For $k>K$, the outward lower endpoint of cell $k$ is
$(2k-1)p_-/4>M_X$; for $k<-K$, its outward upper endpoint is
$-(2|k|-1)p_-/4<-M_X$. Thus every cell enclosure that can intersect $X$ is
in the finite candidate list $-K,\ldots,K$. Use the fixed canonical cells
$[k\pi/2-\pi/4,k\pi/2+\pi/4]$, $k\in\mathbb Z$. Enclose each cell using
exact rational expressions from $P_N$ and let $X_k$ be the interval hull of
its intersection with $X$; do not round candidate-cell or residual endpoints.
Include every cell whose $P_N$ enclosure cannot be ruled out as intersecting
$X$. Certify the residual enclosure $R=X_k-kP_N/2$ satisfies
$R\subseteq[-1,1]$, evaluate the corresponding power
polynomial and add the explicit geometric tail by exact rational interval
arithmetic, then round the final endpoints outward. The tail comes from
[[lem-trigonometric-identities-machin-and-range-reduction]], and map by the
quarter-period identities. Intersect every finite sine/cosine enclosure
with $[-1,1]$, including after the sign and coordinate swaps; the exact
values satisfy these bounds. If the input width is at least $2\sup(P_N)$,
return $[-1,1]$. If a cell cannot be certified in the reduced interval or the
finite candidate list cannot be resolved, return `inconclusive`. For tangent,
divide the sine enclosure by the cosine enclosure only on canonical pieces
where the latter excludes zero; otherwise return `split-domain` or
`inconclusive`.

5. For complex exponential, evaluate real $\exp(X)$, $\cos(Y)$ and
$\sin(Y)$ and combine them by rectangle operations. For principal
$\operatorname{Log}$, require a rectangle excluding zero and every point of
the negative real branch cut; otherwise return `domain-error`. Subdivide into
sign-stable quadrants and axis pieces; on the quadrants use
$$
\operatorname{Arg}(x+iy)=
\begin{cases}
\arctan(y/x),&x>0,\ y>0,\\
-\arctan((-y)/x),&x>0,\ y<0,\\
\pi-\arctan(y/(-x)),&x<0,\ y>0,\\
-\pi+\arctan((-y)/(-x)),&x<0,\ y<0.
\end{cases}
$$
For $x=0,y>0$ set $\operatorname{Arg}(iy)=\pi/2$, for $x=0,y<0$ set it to
$-\pi/2$, and on the positive real axis set it to zero. Enclose
$\ln\sqrt{X^2+Y^2}$ by the real operations and elementary evaluators. If the
branch or sign cannot be certified, return `inconclusive`.

6. Each displayed series uses indices $0,\ldots,N$, hence at most $N+1$
terms; $N$ is the truncation index. Branch breakpoints, dyadic scales and
$P_N$ are fixed by the call parameters, independent of the input box; no
adaptive subdivision or precision refinement is hidden inside this evaluator.

Every finite enclosure returned by
[[alg-certified-elementary-range-evaluation]] for a real interval in the
domain of $\exp$, $\ln$, $\sqrt{\phantom{x}}$, $\arctan$, $\sin$, $\cos$, or
$\tan$ contains the exact range of that function on the represented domain.
If two input intervals are nested and both calls return finite enclosures,
the canonical branch-cell and fixed-term construction in the algorithm makes
the smaller interval's computed enclosure a subset of the larger one's.
An unresolved fixed branch, pole, invalid domain or overflow returns its
stated non-finite status and carries no finite success claim.

For real intervals, complex rectangles or complex balls on which an operation
is defined, enlarging either input enclosure cannot shrink the computed
enclosure: for binary $\circ\in\{+,-,\times,\div\}$, if $X\subseteq X'$ and
$Y\subseteq Y'$, then the computed set enclosure of $X\circ Y$ is contained
in that of $X'\circ Y'$ whenever both are finite results and their domain
restrictions are preserved. The square-root enclosure is inclusion-isotone on
nonnegative intervals. Each finite ball operation in
[[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]] contains the exact ball
image. A `split-domain`, `entire`, `domain-error`, `overflow`, or
`inconclusive` status makes no finite claim. For a finite expression DAG
whose operation nodes all return finite enclosures, every exact node value
from every admissible input assignment belongs to its computed node
enclosure; in particular, the root enclosure contains the exact range. If any
node returns a non-finite status, no finite DAG enclosure is asserted.

suppliers.source_excerpt:
def-cardinal-polynomial-interpolation, Definition: “Let $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\ge0$, let $x_0<\cdots<x_n$ be distinct real nodes, and let $y_0,\ldots,y_n\in\mathbb R$.”

thm-cardinal-polynomial-interpolant-exists-uniquely, Statement: “Then $I_n y$ from [[def-cardinal-polynomial-interpolation]] is the unique real polynomial of degree at most $n$ satisfying $p(x_i)=y_i$ for every $i=0,\ldots,n$.”

thm-barycentric-interpolation-identities, Statement: “At a node $x_i$, the interpolant is defined by the separate value $I_n y(x_i)=y_i$; the quotient is not used there.”

thm-lagrange-interpolation-remainder, Statement: “If $x=x_j$ for a node, then $f(x)-p(x)=0$.” and “If $x\in[a,b]$ is not a node, there is $$\xi\in\bigl(\min\{x,x_0\},\max\{x,x_n\}\bigr)$$ such that $$f(x)-p(x)=\frac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi)}{(n+1)!_{\mathbb R}}\,\omega_n(x).$$”

alg-finite-barycentric-interpolation-evaluator, Definition: “The output is either a record with status *success* and a value in $\mathbb F$, or one of the statuses *invalid_nodes*, *invalid_data*, and *range_failure*.”

prop-finite-barycentric-interpolation-evaluator-returns-status, Statement: “For every input tuple of [[alg-finite-barycentric-interpolation-evaluator]], the procedure terminates and returns one of its declared statuses.”

Assume Countable Choice. Let $1\le p<\infty$, integer $r\ge1$,
integer $s\ge0$, and real-valued $v\in W^{\max(r,s),p}(\widehat S_d)$.
There is a polynomial $q\in\mathbb P_{r-1}(\widehat S_d)$, chosen by
matching all means $\int_{\widehat S_d}D^\alpha q=
\int_{\widehat S_d}D^\alpha v$ for $|\alpha|\le r-1$, such that:

- if $0\le s\le r$, then
  $\|v-q\|_{W^{s,p}(\widehat S_d)}\le C|v|_{W^{r,p}(\widehat S_d)}$;
- if $s>r$, then
  $\|v-q\|_{W^{s,p}(\widehat S_d)}\le
  C\sum_{j=r}^{s}|v|_{W^{j,p}(\widehat S_d)}$.

The second clause assumes $v\in W^{s,p}$; constants depend only on
$d,p,r,s$.

supplier_item_records.excerpt:
def-extended-real-epsilon-subdifferential, Definition: “Let $g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper and convex in the convention of [[def-proper-closed-convex-function-on-rn]]. For $x\in\operatorname{dom}g$ and $\eta\ge0$, define
$$\partial_\eta g(x)=\{p\in\mathbb R^n:g(z)\ge g(x)+\langle p,z-x\rangle-\eta\text{ for every }z\in\mathbb R^n\}.$$
Write $\partial g(x)=\partial_0g(x)$. If $x\notin\operatorname{dom}g$, set $\partial_\eta g(x)=\varnothing$. When $g$ is finite-valued on a convex domain, $\partial g(x)$ agrees with [[def-subgradient-and-subdifferential]].”

def-proper-closed-convex-function-on-rn, Definition: “Let $n\in\mathbb N$ and let $g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$. Its effective domain is $\operatorname{dom}g=\{x:g(x)<+\infty\}$. The function is **proper** if $\operatorname{dom}g\ne\varnothing$; it is **convex** if
$$g((1-\theta)x+\theta y)\le(1-\theta)g(x)+\theta g(y)\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb R^n,\ 0\le\theta\le1),$$
using the endpoint convention $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ of [[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functionals-on-a-banach-space]]. It is **closed** (equivalently, lower semicontinuous in the extended-real convex-analysis convention used here) if its epigraph
$$\operatorname{epi}g=\{(x,s)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R:g(x)\le s\}$$
is closed in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$. The proximal-gradient items on this page assume $g$ is proper, closed and convex.”

def-proximal-mapping, Definition: “Let $g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper, closed and convex, and let $t>0$. For $v\in\mathbb R^n$, define the set-valued proximal mapping
$$\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(v)=\left\{u\in\mathbb R^n:g(u)+\frac{\|u-v\|_2^2}{2t}\le g(w)+\frac{\|w-v\|_2^2}{2t}\text{ for every }w\in\mathbb R^n\right\}.$$
The existence and uniqueness theorem on this page proves that this set is a singleton for every admissible $g,t,v$; its unique member is also denoted $\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(v)$.”

lem-proper-closed-convex-function-affine-minorant, Statement: “Let $n\in\mathbb N$ and let $g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper, closed and convex in the epigraph convention of [[def-proper-closed-convex-function-on-rn]]. Then there are $a\in\mathbb R^n$ and $b\in\mathbb R$ such that
$$g(x)\ge\langle a,x\rangle+b\qquad(x\in\mathbb R^n).$$”

lem-smooth-composite-sum-preserves-proper-closed-convexity, Statement: “Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be continuous and convex, and let $g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper, closed and convex under the epigraph convention of [[def-proper-closed-convex-function-on-rn]]. Then $F=f+g$ is proper, closed and convex in the same convention.”

thm-proximal-operator-existence-resolvent-firm-nonexpansive, Statement: “Let $g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper, closed and convex in the epigraph convention of [[def-proper-closed-convex-function-on-rn]]. For every $t>0$ and $v\in\mathbb R^n$, the set $\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(v)$ is a singleton. Its unique element $u$ satisfies the resolvent equivalence
$$u=\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(v)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (v-u)/t\in\partial g(u).$$
For any $v_1,v_2$ and $u_i=\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(v_i)$,
$$\|u_1-u_2\|_2^2\le\langle u_1-u_2,v_1-v_2\rangle.$$
In particular the proximal map is nonexpansive.”

suppliers.source_excerpt:
def-lasso-estimator, Definition: “For $n,d\ge1$, a deterministic design $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$, response $y\in\mathbb R^n$, and penalty $\tau>0$, define the Lasso objective
$$Q_y(\theta)=\frac1n\|y-X\theta\|_2^2+2\tau\|\theta\|_1.$$
Its minimizer set is $\mathcal M(y)=\operatorname{argmin}_{\theta\in\mathbb R^d}Q_y(\theta)$. The penalty is strictly positive; no full-rank condition on $X$ is imposed. The nonemptiness, compactness, and convexity of this set are proved separately; this page defines the objective and minimizer set but does not select one minimizer.”

lem-lasso-objective-has-minimizer, Statement: “Fix integers $n,d\ge1$, a deterministic matrix $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$, a response $y\in\mathbb R^n$, and a penalty $\tau>0$. The minimizer set $\mathcal M(y)$ of [[def-lasso-estimator]] is nonempty, compact, and convex.”

def-soft-thresholding-function, Definition: “For $\tau>0$ and $z\in\mathbb R$, define the **soft-thresholding map**
$$S_\tau(z)=\begin{cases}z-\tau,&z>\tau,\\0,&-\tau\le z\le\tau,\\z+\tau,&z<-\tau.\end{cases}$$”

ex-orthogonal-design-lasso-is-soft-thresholding, Example: “Let $n\ge d\ge1$, let $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$ satisfy $X^TX=nI_d$, and let $Y\in\mathbb R^n$ be any response. Set $Z=X^TY/n$ and use the penalty $\tau>0$ from [[def-lasso-estimator]]. The unique Lasso minimizer has coordinates $\widehat\theta_j=S_\tau(Z_j)$.”

$$\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(v)=\left\{u\in\mathbb R^n:g(u)+\frac{\|u-v\|_2^2}{2t}\le g(w)+\frac{\|w-v\|_2^2}{2t}\text{ for every }w\in\mathbb R^n\right\}.$$
The existence and uniqueness theorem on this page proves that this set is a singleton for every admissible $g,t,v$; its unique member is also denoted $\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(v)$.”

lem-proper-closed-convex-function-affine-minorant, Statement: “Let $n\in\mathbb N$ and let $g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper, closed and convex in the epigraph convention of [[def-proper-closed-convex-function-on-rn]]. Then there are $a\in\mathbb R^n$ and $b\in\mathbb R$ such that
$$g(x)\ge\langle a,x\rangle+b\qquad(x\in\mathbb R^n).$$”

lem-smooth-composite-sum-preserves-proper-closed-convexity, Statement: “Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be continuous and convex, and let $g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper, closed and convex under the epigraph convention of [[def-proper-closed-convex-function-on-rn]]. Then $F=f+g$ is proper, closed and convex in the same convention.”

thm-proximal-operator-existence-resolvent-firm-nonexpansive, Statement: “Let $g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper, closed and convex in the epigraph convention of [[def-proper-closed-convex-function-on-rn]]. For every $t>0$ and $v\in\mathbb R^n$, the set $\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(v)$ is a singleton. Its unique element $u$ satisfies the resolvent equivalence
$$u=\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(v)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (v-u)/t\in\partial g(u).$$

$$\|u_1-u_2\|_2^2\le\langle u_1-u_2,v_1-v_2\rangle.$$

$$\partial_\eta g(x)=\{p\in\mathbb R^n:g(z)\ge g(x)+\langle p,z-x\rangle-\eta\text{ for every }z\in\mathbb R^n\}.$$
Write $\partial g(x)=\partial_0g(x)$. If $x\notin\operatorname{dom}g$, set $\partial_\eta g(x)=\varnothing$. When $g$ is finite-valued on a convex domain, $\partial g(x)$ agrees with [[def-subgradient-and-subdifferential]].”

def-proper-closed-convex-function-on-rn, Definition: “Let $n\in\mathbb N$ and let $g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$. Its effective domain is $\operatorname{dom}g=\{x:g(x)<+\infty\}$. The function is **proper** if $\operatorname{dom}g\ne\varnothing$; it is **convex** if
$$g((1-\theta)x+\theta y)\le(1-\theta)g(x)+\theta g(y)\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb R^n,\ 0\le\theta\le1),$$

original.source_excerpt:
def-lasso-estimator, Definition: “For $n,d\ge1$, a deterministic design $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$, response $y\in\mathbb R^n$, and penalty $\tau>0$, define the Lasso objective
$$Q_y(\theta)=\frac1n\|y-X\theta\|_2^2+2\tau\|\theta\|_1.$$
Its minimizer set is $\mathcal M(y)=\operatorname{argmin}_{\theta\in\mathbb R^d}Q_y(\theta)$. The penalty is strictly positive; no full-rank condition on $X$ is imposed. The nonemptiness, compactness, and convexity of this set are proved separately; this page defines the objective and minimizer set but does not select one minimizer.”

lem-lasso-objective-has-minimizer, Statement: “Fix integers $n,d\ge1$, a deterministic matrix $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$, a response $y\in\mathbb R^n$, and a penalty $\tau>0$. The minimizer set $\mathcal M(y)$ of [[def-lasso-estimator]] is nonempty, compact, and convex.”

def-soft-thresholding-function, Definition: “For $\tau>0$ and $z\in\mathbb R$, define the **soft-thresholding map**
$$S_\tau(z)=\begin{cases}z-\tau,&z>\tau,\\0,&-\tau\le z\le\tau,\\z+\tau,&z<-\tau.\end{cases}$$”

ex-orthogonal-design-lasso-is-soft-thresholding, Example: “Let $n\ge d\ge1$, let $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$ satisfy $X^TX=nI_d$, and let $Y\in\mathbb R^n$ be any response. Set $Z=X^TY/n$ and use the penalty $\tau>0$ from [[def-lasso-estimator]]. The unique Lasso minimizer has coordinates $\widehat\theta_j=S_\tau(Z_j)$.”

def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes, Definition:
Fix an integer $d\ge2$. The **reference open simplex** is
$$\widehat S_d:=\{\widehat x\in\mathbb R^d:\widehat x_i>0\ (1\le i\le d),\ \sum_{i=1}^d\widehat x_i<1\},$$
with closure $\overline{\widehat S_d}=\operatorname{conv}\{0,e_1,\ldots,e_d\}$.

A **matching affine simplicial mesh** of a bounded polyhedral open set
$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ is a finite set $\mathcal T$ of closed,
nondegenerate $d$-simplices such that their union is $\overline\Omega$,
their interiors are pairwise disjoint, $\Omega$ is the interior of their
union, and the intersection of two distinct cells is either empty or a
whole face of each. Thus no lower-dimensional crack is omitted from
$\Omega$ while its surrounding cells are retained. Every interior facet is
incident to exactly two cells and every boundary facet to one. The faces of
a cell are the convex hulls of its vertex subsets. A facet means a face of
dimension $d-1$.

For each cell $K\in\mathcal T$, an affine bijection

thm-cea-quasi-optimality-for-conforming-galerkin-approximations, Statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $V$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let
$a:V\times V\to\mathbb K$ be linear in its first argument, conjugate-linear
in its second, bounded by $M$, and coercive with constant $\alpha>0$:
$$|a(v,w)|\le M\|v\|_V\|w\|_V,\qquad \operatorname{Re}a(v,v)\ge\alpha\|v\|_V^2.$$
Let $F:V\to\mathbb K$ be bounded and conjugate-linear, and let $V_h\subseteq V$
be finite-dimensional. Then there are unique $u\in V$ and $u_h\in V_h$ with
$$a(u,v)=F(v)\quad(v\in V).$$
$$a(u_h,v_h)=F(v_h)\quad(v_h\in V_h).$$
The solutions satisfy
$$\|u-u_h\|_V\le\frac M\alpha\inf_{v_h\in V_h}\|u-v_h\|_V.$$
The real bilinear case uses linear functionals and reads $\operatorname{Re}$ as
the identity.

cor-shape-regular-affine-fe-primal-energy-approximation, Statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\ge2$, let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a
bounded polyhedral open set with a matching shape-regular affine simplicial
mesh family $\{\mathcal T_h\}$, and set $h:=\max_{K\in\mathcal T_h}h_K\le1$.
Fix an integer $r\ge1$. On the reference simplex let
$(\widehat S_d,\widehat P,\widehat\Sigma)$ be an unisolvent real scalar
finite element whose polynomial space contains $\mathbb P_r$. Assume each
degree of freedom has a bounded linear extension to
$W^{r+1,2}(\widehat S_d)$, and let $\widehat I$ be its interpolant. Suppose
there is a global map $I_h$ whose restriction to each cell is the affine
pullback of $\widehat I$, and that $I_hu\in V_h$ for the conforming discrete
space $V_h\subset H^1_0(\Omega)$ whenever
$u\in W^{r+1,2}(\Omega)\cap H^1_0(\Omega)$, where $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is the
closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ in $W^{1,2}(\Omega)$
([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]). Then a constant $C$ independent of
$h$ and $u$ satisfies
$$\|u-I_hu\|_{H^1(\Omega)}\le C h^r|u|_{W^{r+1,2}(\Omega)}.$$
The global conformity and zero-boundary mapping property of $I_h$ are explicit
hypotheses; this estimate does not assert them for arbitrary degrees of
freedom.

cor-aubin-nitsche-h-r-plus-s-rate-under-primal-and-dual-approximation, Statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Assume the real scalar finite-element setting of
[[cor-shape-regular-affine-fe-primal-energy-approximation]], and set
$V:=H^1_0(\Omega)$ with its usual $H^1$ norm. Let $V_h\subseteq V$ be the
stated conforming discrete space, let $a:V\times V\to\mathbb R$ be the same
bounded coercive form as in
[[thm-cea-quasi-optimality-for-conforming-galerkin-approximations]], and let
$u\in W^{r+1,2}(\Omega)\cap V$ and $u_h\in V_h$ solve the continuous and
discrete equations for the same bounded linear datum $F:V\to\mathbb R$;
assume also that $V_h$ is finite-dimensional. The natural inclusion
$J:V\to L^2(\Omega)$ obeys $\|Jv\|_{L^2}\le\|v\|_{H^1}$. For
$e:=J(u-u_h)$, let $z_e$ be the adjoint solution from
[[thm-aubin-nitsche-l2-error-estimate-under-adjoint-regularity]]. Suppose
there are $s\in(0,1]$, a normed regularity space $R_s\subseteq V$ for $z_e$,
and constants $C_D,C_R$ independent of $h$ and $e$ such that
$$\|z_e\|_{R_s}\le C_R\|e\|_{L^2(\Omega)}.$$
$$\inf_{w_h\in V_h}\|z_e-w_h\|_{H^1(\Omega)}\le C_D h^s\|z_e\|_{R_s}.$$
Then
$$\|u-u_h\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le \frac{M^2}{\alpha}C_{\rm FE}C_DC_R h^{r+s}|u|_{W^{r+1,2}(\Omega)}.$$
Here $C_{\rm FE}$ is the primal interpolation constant and $M,\alpha$ are
the boundedness and coercivity constants of $a$. In a full-adjoint Poisson
branch, one may take $R_1=H^2(\Omega)\cap H^1_0(\Omega)$ with the $H^2$ norm,
provided both displayed dual bounds hold. The $h^{r+1}$ rate is conditional
on those bounds and the primal approximation bound; no full-adjoint
regularity is asserted on an arbitrary Lipschitz domain.

Let $F:V\to\mathbb K$ be bounded and conjugate-linear, and let $V_h\subseteq V$
be finite-dimensional. Then there are unique $u\in V$ and $u_h\in V_h$ with
$$a(u,v)=F(v)\quad(v\in V).$$
$$a(u_h,v_h)=F(v_h)\quad(v_h\in V_h).$$
The solutions satisfy
$$\|u-u_h\|_V\le\frac M\alpha\inf_{v_h\in V_h}\|u-v_h\|_V.$$
The real bilinear case uses linear functionals and reads $\operatorname{Re}$ as
the identity.

cor-shape-regular-affine-fe-primal-energy-approximation, Statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\ge2$, let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a
bounded polyhedral open set with a matching shape-regular affine simplicial
mesh family $\{\mathcal T_h\}$, and set $h:=\max_{K\in\mathcal T_h}h_K\le1$.
Fix an integer $r\ge1$. On the reference simplex let
$(\widehat S_d,\widehat P,\widehat\Sigma)$ be an unisolvent real scalar
finite element whose polynomial space contains $\mathbb P_r$. Assume each
degree of freedom has a bounded linear extension to
$W^{r+1,2}(\widehat S_d)$, and let $\widehat I$ be its interpolant. Suppose
there is a global map $I_h$ whose restriction to each cell is the affine
pullback of $\widehat I$, and that $I_hu\in V_h$ for the conforming discrete
space $V_h\subset H^1_0(\Omega)$ whenever
$u\in W^{r+1,2}(\Omega)\cap H^1_0(\Omega)$, where $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is the
closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ in $W^{1,2}(\Omega)$
([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]). Then a constant $C$ independent of
$h$ and $u$ satisfies
$$\|u-I_hu\|_{H^1(\Omega)}\le C h^r|u|_{W^{r+1,2}(\Omega)}.$$
The global conformity and zero-boundary mapping property of $I_h$ are explicit
hypotheses; this estimate does not assert them for arbitrary degrees of
freedom.

cor-aubin-nitsche-h-r-plus-s-rate-under-primal-and-dual-approximation, Statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Assume the real scalar finite-element setting of
[[cor-shape-regular-affine-fe-primal-energy-approximation]], and set
$V:=H^1_0(\Omega)$ with its usual $H^1$ norm. Let $V_h\subseteq V$ be the
stated conforming discrete space, let $a:V\times V\to\mathbb R$ be the same
bounded coercive form as in
[[thm-cea-quasi-optimality-for-conforming-galerkin-approximations]], and let
$u\in W^{r+1,2}(\Omega)\cap V$ and $u_h\in V_h$ solve the continuous and
discrete equations for the same bounded linear datum $F:V\to\mathbb R$;
assume also that $V_h$ is finite-dimensional. The natural inclusion
$J:V\to L^2(\Omega)$ obeys $\|Jv\|_{L^2}\le\|v\|_{H^1}$. For
$e:=J(u-u_h)$, let $z_e$ be the adjoint solution from
[[thm-aubin-nitsche-l2-error-estimate-under-adjoint-regularity]]. Suppose
there are $s\in(0,1]$, a normed regularity space $R_s\subseteq V$ for $z_e$,
and constants $C_D,C_R$ independent of $h$ and $e$ such that
$$\|z_e\|_{R_s}\le C_R\|e\|_{L^2(\Omega)}.$$
$$\inf_{w_h\in V_h}\|z_e-w_h\|_{H^1(\Omega)}\le C_D h^s\|z_e\|_{R_s}.$$
Then
$$\|u-u_h\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le \frac{M^2}{\alpha}C_{\rm FE}C_DC_R h^{r+s}|u|_{W^{r+1,2}(\Omega)}.$$
Here $C_{\rm FE}$ is the primal interpolation constant and $M,\alpha$ are
the boundedness and coercivity constants of $a$. In a full-adjoint Poisson
branch, one may take $R_1=H^2(\Omega)\cap H^1_0(\Omega)$ with the $H^2$ norm,
provided both displayed dual bounds hold. The $h^{r+1}$ rate is conditional
on those bounds and the primal approximation bound; no full-adjoint
regularity is asserted on an arbitrary Lipschitz domain.

$$V_h^{\mathrm{conf}}:=\{v\in V_h^{\mathrm{br}}:v|_{F,K}=v|_{F,K'}\text{ on every interior facet }F\}.$$”

supplier_excerpts.excerpt: A **real interval** is a closed set $[a,b]\subset\mathbb R$ with finite dyadic endpoints $a\le b$. Its width is $b-a$, midpoint is $(a+b)/2$, and its midpoint-radius form is $m+[-r,r]$ with $m=(a+b)/2$ and $r=(b-a)/2$. The empty set is the status `empty`; the whole real line is `entire`. `overflow`, `domain-error`, `split-domain`, and `inconclusive` are computation statuses, not finite intervals.

Supplier definition excerpt: “1. Reduce $A$ to upper Hessenberg form with Householder similarities. For $k=1,\ldots,\max(n-2,0)$ in increasing order, use active indices $S=\{k+1,\ldots,n\}$, target $x=H_{S,k}$, and trailing left panel $B=H_{S,\{k+1,\ldots,n\}}$ with columns in increasing order. In the real branch use [[alg-scaled-householder-reflector-formation-and-application]] for the finite left application and overwrite; in the complex branch use [[alg-complex-scaled-householder-reflector-step]]. Complete each similarity by the right application above on columns $S$. If the resulting matrix fails the exact upper-Hessenberg zero-pattern check, return bulge-chase-invariant-failure with the partial factors. Store the exact unitary reflector factors as a product representation $Q_0$.
2. At each sweep, test every active first-subdiagonal entry by
   $$|h_{i,i-1}|\le\tau\bigl(|h_{i-1,i-1}|+|h_{i,i}|\bigr).$$
   For a complex entry $z=a+ib$, evaluate $|z|$ by $s=\max(|a|,|b|)$ and $s\sqrt{(a/s)^2+(b/s)^2}$ when $z\ne0$, with divisions, squares, sum, square root and final scaling rounded in the stated order; use $|0|=0$. Return range-failure if this evaluation fails. Compute the diagonal-magnitude sum first, then multiply by $\tau$ in the operationwise model; compare the resulting finite values exactly. When the test holds, set that entry to zero, record its original value as a deflation perturbation, and split the active block. The equality case deflates. Do not use the Hermitian-tridiagonal Wilkinson shift rule for a general Hessenberg matrix.
3. Check for the target Schur block structure after initialization and after each sweep. A complex active block of size at least two uses a single shift, normally its bottom-right entry. A real active block of size at least two uses the real quadratic $p(z)=z^2-sz+t$ with trailing block $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$; compute $s=\operatorname{fl}(a+d)$ and $t=\operatorname{fl}(\operatorname{fl}(ad)-\operatorname{fl}(bc))$ in that order, returning range-failure if an operation fails. Maintain a counter for each active block, reset it after any deflation in that block, and after $h$ consecutive sweeps without deflation consume that block's next declared exceptional shift or real quadratic. If the required table entry is absent, return stagnation-exhausted.
4. Apply the corresponding implicit bulge chase from [[alg-exact-francis-hessenberg-qr-step]]. For the initial single-shift vector compute $x_1=\operatorname{fl}(h_{11}-\mu)$ and $x_i=h_{i1}$ for $i>1$. For the initial real double-shift vector, compute $u=He_1$, then $w=Hu$ by left-to-right rounded matrix-vector products, then $x=\operatorname{fl}(\operatorname{fl}(w-su)+te_1)$ componentwise. Compute only the first $r+1$ components from the Hessenberg support pattern; on range failure return the operation index and partial factors. For a chase at column $j$, use active indices $S=I_j$, target $x=H_{S,j}$, and trailing left panel $B=H_{S,\{j+1,\ldots,n\}}$ with columns in increasing order. Call the real or complex formation routine, write the target tail zeros exactly, complete the two-sided update by the right-kernel order above on columns $S$, and append the exact reflector representation to $Q$. In the initial polynomial-vector step there is no matrix-target column; use the full active row panel for the left update and then apply the right update to its active columns. If the exact routine or its finite-precision realization returns bulge-chase-invariant-failure, return that status with the partial matrix and factors. Use [[lem-two-sided-scaled-householder-similarity-error]] to store the proved two-sided coefficient $\alpha_{m_j}=a_{m_j}+b_{m_j}+a_{m_j}b_{m_j}$, with $a$ the target-overwrite coefficient or separate-block coefficient as actually used and $b$ the right separate-block coefficient. This gives $\|E_j\|_F\le\alpha_{m_j}\|\widehat H_{j-1}\|_F$ when its $m_ju<1$ and range hypotheses hold. Apply the same certificate to every Hessenberg-initialization similarity. If any step lacks that certificate, retain the residual diagnostic and set the backward-error-certificate status to inconclusive.
5. Stop with Schur-computed when every complex block has size one, or every real block has size one or is a $2\times2$ block with negative characteristic-polynomial discriminant. supplier_excerpts.excerpt:
Assume AC. Let $d,m\ge1$ be finite, fix $T>0$, and work on a complete filtered
probability space whose filtration is right-continuous and contains every
$P$-null subset of $\mathcal F$ in $\mathcal F_0$. Let $W=(W_t)_{0\le t\le T}$
be an adapted standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion whose increments are
independent of the current filtration. Let
$X_0$ be finite and $\mathcal F_0$-measurable, independent of
$\sigma(W_t-W_0:0\le t\le T)$. Use Euclidean state norms and the Frobenius
matrix norm. Consider
the autonomous SDE
$$X_t=X_0+\int_0^t f(X_s)\,ds+\int_0^t g(X_s)\,dW_s, \qquad X_t\in\mathbb R^d,$$
where $f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ and
$g:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}$ are $C^1$. Assume that constants
$\mu,c,D\ge0$ and an integer $q\ge1$ satisfy, for all $x,y\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$\langle x-y,f(x)-f(y)\rangle\le\mu|x-y|^2, \qquad \|g(x)-g(y)\|_F^2\le c|x-y|^2,$$
and
$$|f(x)-f(y)|^2\le D(1+|x|^q+|y|^q)|x-y|^2.$$
For each $0<h\le1$ with $N=T/h\in\mathbb N$, let $Y^h$ be the continuous
Euler–Maruyama interpolation and $\bar Y^h$ its left-endpoint step process
from [[alg-euler-maruyama-autonomous]]. Assume
that an exact strong solution $X$ and these exact, step and continuous Euler
processes have uniformly bounded moments of every finite order on $[0,T]$:
for every $p\ge1$,
$$\mathbb E\sup_{t\le T}|X_t|^p+ \sup_{0<h\le1,\ T/h\in\mathbb N}\left( \mathbb E\sup_{t\le T}|Y_t^h|^p+ \mathbb E\sup_{t\le T}|\bar Y_t^h|^p\right)<\infty.$$
Then a constant $C$, independent of $h$, satisfies
$$\mathbb E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|X_t-Y_t^h|^2\le Ch.$$
In particular the grid-point root-mean-square error is $O(h^{1/2})$.
The all-moment premise is part of this source contract; $X_0\in L^2$ alone
does not imply it.

supplier_items.source_excerpt:
For every $n\in\mathbb N$ and reals $c_0,\ldots,c_n$, the function
$$q(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}c_kx^k$$
is the evaluation of a formal real polynomial of degree at most $n$. The representative can be chosen so that it is the zero polynomial exactly when every $c_k=0$; if $c_n\ne0$, it has degree $n$ and leading coefficient $c_n$. Here the coefficient vector may be padded by zeros for the displayed sum; padding describes the evaluation, not a change to the formal polynomial object.

For every $n\in\mathbb N$ and reals $r_0,\ldots,r_{n-1}$, the function
$$P_n(X)=\prod_{k<n}(X-r_k)$$
is the evaluation of a formal real polynomial of degree exactly $n$ with leading coefficient $1$. For $n=0$ the product is empty and equals $1$.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\ge0$, let $x_0<\cdots<x_n$ be distinct real nodes, and let $y_0,\ldots,y_n\in\mathbb R$. Define the node polynomial and barycentric weights by
$$\omega_n(X)=\prod_{k=0}^{n}(X-x_k),\qquad w_j=\left(\prod_{\substack{0\le k\le n\\k\ne j}}(x_j-x_k)\right)^{-1}\quad(0\le j\le n).$$

subnormal is $\eta$, the smallest positive normal is $2^{e_{\min}}$, and the
largest finite magnitude is $N_{\max}$. The extended endpoint set also contains

numbers.

suppliers.source_excerpt:
Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.
suppliers.evidence: Actual typed interface inspected and used only with its field/dimension/choice hypotheses; real transfer is proved locally, not assumed from complex calculus. No mathematical acceptance or new readiness claim.

suppliers.source_excerpt:
A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.
suppliers.evidence: Actual typed interface inspected and used only with its field/dimension/choice hypotheses; real transfer is proved locally, not assumed from complex calculus. No mathematical acceptance or new readiness claim.

suppliers.source_excerpt:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

suppliers.source_excerpt:
Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

original.source_excerpt:
Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

original.source_excerpt:
A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

original.source_excerpt:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

suppliers.required_interface: Local cellwise W^{1,2} interpolation error: for 1≤ell≤r≤k+1 and m=1, the error is bounded by C h_K^{r-1}|u|_{W^{r,2}(K)} on the stated shape-regular affine meshes; a globally conforming interpolant and boundary preservation remain explicit consumer assumptions.
suppliers.source_excerpt:
thm-local-finite-element-interpolation-estimates, theorem: “Assume Countable Choice. Let $k\ge0$, $1\le p<\infty$, and let
$(\widehat S_d,\widehat P,\widehat\Sigma)$ be a reference finite element
whose polynomial space contains $\mathbb P_k$. Assume its degrees of
freedom are bounded on $W^{\ell,p}(\widehat S_d)$ for an integer
$\ell\ge1$, let $r,m\in\mathbb N_0$, and let $\widehat I$ be its
interpolant. Thus
$\widehat Iq=q$ for $q\in\mathbb P_k$. On a shape-regular affine mesh
as in [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]], for each cell $K$ with its
orientation-preserving reference map $F_K$ define
$$I_Kv=(\widehat I(v\circ F_K))\circ F_K^{-1}.$$
For every such cell, if $\ell\le r\le k+1$ and $0\le m\le r$, then for
$v\in W^{r,p}(K)$,
$$|v-I_Kv|_{W^{m,p}(K)}\le C h_K^{r-m}|v|_{W^{r,p}(K)}.$$
If $\ell>k+1$ and $0\le m\le k+1$, then for $v\in W^{\ell,p}(K)$,
$$|v-I_Kv|_{W^{m,p}(K)} \le C\sum_{n=k+1}^{\ell}h_K^{n-m}|v|_{W^{n,p}(K)}.$$
The constants are uniform over the mesh family and depend on the stated
reference element, exponents and shape-regularity bound. For Lagrange
elements, the boundedness hypothesis on the nodal functionals is supplied
by [[thm-lagrange-point-evaluation-threshold-on-reference-simplex]] when
$\ell>d/p$; unisolvence of a particular node set is a separate hypothesis.”

suppliers.source_excerpt:
thm-cea-quasi-optimality-for-conforming-galerkin-approximations, theorem: “Assume Countable Choice. Let $V$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let
$a:V\times V\to\mathbb K$ be linear in its first argument, conjugate-linear
in its second, bounded by $M$, and coercive with constant $\alpha>0$:
$$|a(v,w)|\le M\|v\|_V\|w\|_V,\qquad \operatorname{Re}a(v,v)\ge\alpha\|v\|_V^2.$$
Let $F:V\to\mathbb K$ be bounded and conjugate-linear, and let $V_h\subseteq V$
be finite-dimensional. Then there are unique $u\in V$ and $u_h\in V_h$ with
$$a(u,v)=F(v)\quad(v\in V).$$
$$a(u_h,v_h)=F(v_h)\quad(v_h\in V_h).$$
The solutions satisfy
$$\|u-u_h\|_V\le\frac M\alpha\inf_{v_h\in V_h}\|u-v_h\|_V.$$
The real bilinear case uses linear functionals and reads $\operatorname{Re}$ as
the identity.”

suppliers.required_interface: For bounded polyhedral D, H0^1(D) with the W^{1,2} norm is a separable real Hilbert space under Countable Choice; its gradient norm is equivalent by Poincare and therefore gives an equivalent complete Hilbert norm.
suppliers.source_excerpt:
lem-parabolic-zero-boundary-sobolev-space-is-separable, lemma: “Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded
polyhedral open set with $d\ge1$. Put
$$H=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R),\qquad V=W^{1,2}_0(\Omega;\mathbb R),\qquad \|v\|_V=\|v\|_{W^{1,2}(\Omega)}.$$
Then $V$ is a separable real Hilbert space, and the inclusion
$V\hookrightarrow H$ is continuous, injective and dense. Consequently
$(V,H,V^*)$ is a real evolution triple in the sense of
[[def-parabolic-evolution-triple-and-energy-space]]. The gradient norm
$\|\nabla v\|_{L^2}$ is equivalent to this norm on $V$ by Poincare's
inequality.”

suppliers.source_excerpt:
def-coordinatewise-product-moment-functional, definition: “For $d\ge1$, let $(a_j,b_j,m_j,2m_j-1,\mu_j)$ be Gaussian moment data for
each coordinate $j=1,\ldots,d$, and write
$M^{(j)}_k:=\int x^k\,d\mu_j(x)$. A **coordinatewise tensor polynomial** is a
finite coefficient family $(c_\alpha)$ indexed by multi-indices
$\alpha=(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_d)$ with
$0\le\alpha_j\le2m_j-1$, evaluated by
$$ P(x_1,\ldots,x_d)=\sum_{\alpha}c_\alpha\prod_{j=1}^{d}x_j^{\alpha_j}. $$
Define its **coordinatewise product-moment value** by
$$ I_\otimes(P):=\sum_{\alpha}c_\alpha\prod_{j=1}^{d}M^{(j)}_{\alpha_j}. $$
The coefficient family is part of the formal polynomial data, so this finite
sum is unambiguous. This definition specifies the product-moment functional
used for coordinatewise exactness without requiring a measure-product
construction.”

def-tensor-product-gauss-rule, definition: “Let $d\ge1$ and, for each coordinate $j=1,\ldots,d$, let
$Q_j(f)=\sum_{i=1}^{m_j}w_i^{(j)}f(x_i^{(j)})$ be a well-defined Gaussian rule
as in [[def-gauss-quadrature-rule]] and
[[lem-gauss-quadrature-rule-data-well-defined]]. Its **tensor-product
quadrature rule** is
$$ Q_{\otimes}(f):= \sum_{i_1=1}^{m_1}\cdots\sum_{i_d=1}^{m_d} \left(\prod_{j=1}^{d}w_{i_j}^{(j)}\right) f\left(x_{i_1}^{(1)},\ldots,x_{i_d}^{(d)}\right). $$
Its node set is the Cartesian product of the one-dimensional node sets; the
displayed finite sum is its value on any function defined on that node set.”

thm-gauss-rule-exact-through-degree-2m-minus-1-and-positive-weights, theorem: “Let $(a,b,m,2m-1,\mu)$ be moment data as in
[[def-gauss-moment-data]], and let $Q_m$ and $w_i$ be the rule and weights of
[[def-gauss-quadrature-rule]]. For every real polynomial $f$ of degree at most
$2m-1$,
$$ \int_{[a,b]} f(x)\,d\mu(x)=Q_m(f)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_if(x_i). $$
Moreover, $w_i>0$ for every $i$ and $\sum_iw_i=\mu([a,b])$.”

thm-tensor-product-gauss-exactness-and-exponential-node-count, theorem: “For $d\ge1$, take one-dimensional Gaussian rules $Q_j$ with orders $m_j$ and
moment data $(a_j,b_j,m_j,2m_j-1,\mu_j)$, and form their tensor rule
$Q_\otimes$ as in [[def-tensor-product-gauss-rule]]. For every coordinatewise
tensor polynomial $P$ of [[def-coordinatewise-product-moment-functional]],
$$ Q_\otimes(P)=I_\otimes(P). $$
The tensor rule has exactly $\prod_{j=1}^{d}m_j$ distinct nodes. In particular,
using the same $m\ge2$ nodes in each coordinate requires $m^d$ node
evaluations, exponential growth in $d$.”
